strengths: TaDSE addresses a relevant NLP problem: using available slot annotations to improve dialogue utterance embeddings without collecting sentence-pair similarity labels. The template augmentation and contrastive objectives form an understandable, practically motivated approach.

The experiments provide promising evidence across five intent-classification datasets. Table 2 reports 83.87 average accuracy versus 81.82 for DSE. Table 4 also shows improvements beyond augmentation-only training: adding template and pairwise losses raises SNIPS accuracy from 93.29 to 96.14 and ATIS from 86.00 to 89.59.

The paper examines augmentation strength, individual loss components, the template projection, and inference-time compression. Testing automatically extracted, noisy templates on CLINC150 is useful, and reporting compression failures on some datasets provides a more informative picture than reporting only successful configurations. Public datasets, the initialization checkpoint, and several training settings are identified.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol leaves consequential ambiguities. Appendix C specifies 'full utterance/template training set representations' without clearly identifying whether the nearest-neighbor reference pool contains original utterances, synthetic utterances, templates, or identical resources for every baseline. It is also unclear whether held-out templates for semantic compression use gold annotations or predicted slots. These choices can affect accuracy independently of encoder quality. Because four datasets supply manual slot annotations, the unsupervised claim should explicitly mean training without intent or sentence-pair labels.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the configuration appendix. The three contrastive temperatures, projection architecture, optimizer settings, and embedding normalization procedure are insufficiently specified. Equations 1–2 also place unperturbed representations, including the anchor itself, in the denominator rather than clearly identifying the dropout-positive candidate set. This may be a notation error, but the implemented objective needs clarification. Code is promised only after acceptance.

The pairwise objective has an unresolved false-negative issue. Different augmented utterances can share the same template, yet Equation 3 treats other utterances in the batch as negatives. Selecting distinct utterance strings does not eliminate these semantic collisions. The paper should specify whether sampling or masking prevents them and explain how the objective supports the claimed grouping of utterances sharing a template.

Statistical reliability and model selection need stronger documentation. No repeated-run variability or significance analysis supports the claimed significant improvements. Several compression gains correspond to only a few test examples. Appendix D uses test-set learning curves to motivate different training durations, including longer training for the projection variant; the paper should establish that checkpoint and hyperparameter decisions used validation data and distinguish projection effects from additional training.

Semantic compression is not sufficiently validated as a measure of semantic well-formedness. Interpolating utterances toward a shared template mechanically contracts their pairwise distances before normalization, so improved alignment does not independently establish better semantic structure. Separate t-SNE plots provide limited additional evidence. Normalization details and suitable controls are needed, especially because Table 5 shows small gains on SNIPS/ATIS and frequent degradation on MASSIVE/CLINC150.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Evaluation covers one downstream task using a full labeled nearest-neighbor reference set, without directly testing the low-annotation motivation or broader dialogue capabilities. Contemporary API embeddings are compared on only two datasets, and newer dialogue work cited in the paper is absent from the main comparison. The reported gains make this a plausible Findings contribution, but unresolved evaluation, reproducibility, and model-selection questions prevent a clear positive recommendation.
